analysis.one_liner: Bars prescription drug makers from gouging prices on drugs covered by federal health programs.
analysis.headline: The CURE High Drug Prices Act died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned prescription drug manufacturers from raising prices in a way that far outpaces any real cost increase, when patients cannot avoid the price because there is not enough competition. It set clear triggers: a price rise of 10% in one year, 20% in three years, or 30% in five years would be presumed price gouging. A drug company found to have gouged could be ordered to refund the excess to patients and insurers, sell at the old price for up to a year, or pay a penalty of up to three times the excessive amount. The bill never moved past its first committee stop and expired when the 2019-2020 Congress ended. [S2] [S3] [S5]
analysis.who_benefits: Patients on Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal health programs, along with the insurers and employers who pay part of their drug bills, would gain if a manufacturer's price hikes were clawed back. All consumers would benefit indirectly from a deterrent against steep price increases on widely used drugs. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and payers on federal drug programs

how_it_helps.text: Defines price gouging as a price increase far beyond any justified rise in production or access-expansion costs, which consumers cannot avoid because of insufficient competition. [S3]

Presumes gouging when a drug's price rises 10% or more in 12 months, 20% or more in 36 months, or 30% or more in 60 months, giving regulators a bright line instead of leaving it to judgment alone. [S3]

Lets the Health and Human Services Secretary order a manufacturer to refund the excessive amounts to consumers and third-party payors, hold the price for up to a year, or pay a civil penalty of up to three times the excessive amount if the violation was knowing or repeated. [S3]
Allows the Attorney General to enforce orders in court and to subpoena documents or testimony. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers whose drugs are covered by federal health programs would bear the cost: refunding excessive price increases, selling at pre-hike prices for up to a year, and civil penalties for knowing or repeat violations. If deterred price increases would otherwise have funded higher revenues, that forgone revenue is the industry's cost. [S3]

drawbacks.text: The 10% one-year presumption could flag increases that have legitimate explanations, such as manufacturing cost spikes or investments in expanding access, though the bill allows manufacturers to submit a statement of justification before any penalty. [S3]

The remedy is backward-looking — refunds, temporary price holds, and penalties for knowing violations — rather than a hard cap, so a company could still raise prices and pay after the fact if it accepted the risk. [S3]
The bill only covers drugs within reach of federal health care programs, leaving price increases on drugs sold mainly outside those programs unaddressed. [S3]
Lower revenues from flagship drugs could reduce what manufacturers reinvest in research; the bill includes no offsetting mechanism to ensure research spending. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a concrete deterrent against the steep, competition-proof price increases that have driven drug costs up for patients and public programs, with a refund mechanism that returns money actually taken. The main costs fall on drug makers, and the strongest objection — that a 10% trigger may penalize some justified increases — is softened by the justification process built into the bill. The remedies are narrower than a price cap, which limits both the benefit and the risk. On balance the bill's benefits to patients and payers outweigh its costs, but it never got far enough for Congress to weigh or refine them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to its Health Subcommittee, and then sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and not one cosponsor. [S5] [S4]

narrative.text: Rep. Chellie Pingree introduced the bill on August 2, 2019, calling it the CURE High Drug Prices Act. [S1] [S3]
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and three days later to the committee's Health Subcommittee. [S5]
No further action was ever taken; the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021. [S5]
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: no federal mechanism was created to force refunds or penalties for steep price increases on drugs covered by federal programs, and existing price-setting practice continued unchanged. [S3] [S5]

for.name: Rep. Chellie Pingree
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; it drew no cosponsors from either party.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for health legislation
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up: no hearing, no markup, no vote, leaving it in the Health Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member besides the sponsor signed on, so the bill's partisan shape was never tested. [S4] [S5]

industries.note: The bill would have let regulators claw back price increases on federal-program drugs that far exceed cost growth, with refunds, temporary price holds, and penalties of up to triple the excess. Those steep, competition-proof increases have been a major source of industry revenue and of rising drug costs for patients and public programs. [S2] [S3]
The bill named third-party payors among those entitled to refunds of excessive amounts paid after a gouging determination, recovering costs they pass to customers through premiums. [S3]
